gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured usable capacity or idle draw for any 5,000 W-class unit: HOBOTECH got 4,450 Wh AC (88%) from the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus and 5,390 Wh (88%) from the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra, The Solar Lab measured 84% for the Anker F3800 Plus and the Pecron F5000LFP, and inverter-on idle draw ranges from about 52 W (DELTA Pro Ultra, Pecron) to 85 W (Jackery) and about 112 W (F3800 Plus, Zelpio).
standout_why: I opened both cited pages (solarwaypoint.com, holdbackup.com) and two uncited results (powerbencher.com, thewattguide.com); all four hold maker specs and arithmetic only, and three say outright that they tested nothing. ChatGPT's own answer says its runtimes are 'calculations, not measured runtimes'. None gives a measured Wh, efficiency, idle draw, surge hold or fan noise. I did not open the other uncited results (runtimewise, thiswatt, enoughwatts, wattsift, theoutageplan, homepowerfacts, powersized, power-specs, the maker pages); popularmechanics.com refused the fetch, and its subject, the Anker S5000, is a 4,500 W unit below this page's line.
decides: It confirms ChatGPT's order on runtime and adds a standby ranking, but it does not back a Dealectric pick. At a 5,000 W load the measured energy works out to about 65 min for the DELTA Pro Ultra, 53 min for the Jackery 5000 Plus, about 52 min for the Pecron F5000LFP and about 39 min for the F3800 Plus. Idle draw reorders them for outage standby: with the inverter left on, the Jackery burns about 2,060 Wh a day (41% of its battery), the F3800 Plus about 2,700 Wh (70%), the DELTA Pro Ultra about 1,268 Wh (21%). The two units Dealectric links in this line get little support: the F3800 Plus has the lowest measured efficiency and highest idle draw of the group, and I found no independent measurement of the Nature's Generator L6000. The EcoFlow TITAN 5000 Plus has none either. The page can use these as a named-measurement column, but must say the L6000 row is maker figures only.

findings.label: Measured usable AC capacity (HOBOTECH)
findings.value: 4,450 Wh at 120 V and 4,440 Wh at 240 V, 88% of the rated 5,040 Wh
findings.source_title: The Biggest Jackery Ever: Explorer 5000 Plus Home Backup Solar Generator (HOBOTECH)
findings.note: Posted 2024-11-25 by HOBOTECH Tom. Full discharge through the AC outlets; the page does not state the test load. My arithmetic: 4,450 Wh / 5,000 W = 0.89 h, about 53 min at a constant 5,000 W, assuming the same energy is delivered at that load.

findings.label: Idle draw, inverter on, no load (HOBOTECH)
findings.value: 85 W; 515 Wh used over 6 hours, about 2,060 Wh over 24 hours
findings.source_title: The Biggest Jackery Ever: Explorer 5000 Plus Home Backup Solar Generator (HOBOTECH)
findings.note: Posted 2024-11-25. 2,060 Wh is 41% of 5,040 Wh per day (my arithmetic). The 12 V and USB outputs used 0 Wh over 12 hours at idle. The same post gives the DELTA Pro Ultra as 52 W at idle.

findings.label: Idle draw, inverter on, no load (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: about 58 W; about 3.5 days of idling on a full charge
findings.source_title: Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus Review: Real Competition for the Anker F3800 and DELTA Pro Ultra? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The page shows no publication date. Measured by letting the unit run down from full with the inverter on and nothing plugged in. It disagrees with HOBOTECH's 85 W; give both with names. The same page puts the original Anker F3800 at 80 W idle.

findings.label: Sustained output and surge (HOBOTECH)
findings.value: Held 3,600 W at 120 V and 7,200 W at 240 V for 5 minutes (pass); peak 4,800 W at 120 V and 9,300 W at 240 V for under 5 s
findings.source_title: The Biggest Jackery Ever: Explorer 5000 Plus Home Backup Solar Generator (HOBOTECH)
findings.note: Posted 2024-11-25. This is the only independent check found that a unit in the line holds its full rated output, and only for 5 minutes. Jackery states a 14,400 W surge; HOBOTECH's peak was 9,300 W.

findings.label: Surge test (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: Ran 8,000 W and 9,500 W loads for 20 to 30 seconds; struggled to start an air conditioner with a 10,000 W starting surge
findings.source_title: Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus Review (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: No publication date on the page. The air conditioner's running draw was 3,000 W. Supports ChatGPT's caveat that 7,200 W does not cover every motor start.

findings.label: Fan noise, AC recharge and UPS (HOBOTECH)
findings.value: Inverter fan 44 dB; charging fan 43 dB at maximum, 42 dB at minimum; 120 V charging 1,750 W measured, about 3.5 hours to full; UPS 20 ms backup, 0 ms online (both pass)
findings.source_title: The Biggest Jackery Ever: Explorer 5000 Plus Home Backup Solar Generator (HOBOTECH)
findings.note: Posted 2024-11-25. The page gives no measuring distance for the dB figures. 240 V charging at 4,000 W in 1.7 hours needs Jackery's Smart Transfer Switch; that line reads as the maker's figure, not a timed test.

findings.label: Measured usable capacity (HOBOTECH)
findings.value: AC 5,390 Wh, 88% of the rated 6,144 Wh; DC 5,000 Wh, 81%
findings.source_title: Ecoflow Delta Pro ULTRA 7200w 120v/240v Home Backup Battery Solar Power Generator (HOBOTECH)
findings.note: Posted 2024-01-11 by HOBOTECH Tom; one inverter plus one battery. The DC test ran about 24 hours. My arithmetic: 5,390 Wh / 5,000 W = 1.08 h, about 65 min at 5,000 W (ChatGPT estimated 'about an hour').

findings.label: Idle draw, inverter on, no load (HOBOTECH)
findings.value: 634 Wh over 12 hours, about 53 W; about 1,268 Wh over 24 hours
findings.source_title: Ecoflow Delta Pro ULTRA 7200w 120v/240v Home Backup Battery Solar Power Generator (HOBOTECH)
findings.note: Posted 2024-01-11. The watt figure is my division (634 / 12); HOBOTECH's later Jackery post states 52 W. 1,268 Wh is 21% of 6,144 Wh per day. HOBOTECH says the inverter left on would empty the battery in about 4.5 days.

findings.label: Sustained output, surge and fan noise (HOBOTECH)
findings.value: 5-minute sustained test passed at 6,400 W and failed above it; peak 7,900 W for under 5 s; inverter fan 42 dB
findings.source_title: Ecoflow Delta Pro ULTRA 7200w 120v/240v Home Backup Battery Solar Power Generator (HOBOTECH)
findings.note: Posted 2024-01-11. The page reports a sine-wave check at 120 V only and gives no 240 V load results, so the 6,400 W ceiling may reflect the reviewer's 120 V setup, not the unit's 240 V limit. It still clears 5,000 W. With one battery, The Solar Lab's Ultra X review says output is capped at 6,000 W on that newer model.

findings.label: Runtime near full load, surge and wall charging (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 59 minutes at a load just under 6,000 W (the site calls it 98% efficiency); held 9,200 W for about 10 s; a 120 V wall charge took 4 h 4 min and drew 7.25 kWh
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra real-world testing (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: No publication date on the page. The 98% is figured against a 6,000 Wh battery and an unstated exact load, and it conflicts with HOBOTECH's 88%; quote the 59 minutes, not the percentage. It is the only timed run near the question's 5,000 W found for any candidate besides the original F3800.

findings.label: Idle draw (The Solar Lab)
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X home backup unit (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: No publication date on the page. Stated in passing in the review of the newer Ultra X (which idled at about 36 W); the same page puts the original Anker F3800 near 80 W.

findings.label: Measured efficiency (The Solar Lab)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus (The Solar Lab test results page)
findings.note: No publication date; credited to Cody and Robbie, The Solar Lab. Measured by pushing the 6,000 W inverter from a full battery. My arithmetic: 0.84 x 3,840 Wh = about 3,226 Wh, about 39 min at 5,000 W (ChatGPT estimated 38 to 41 min). The page also says the unit took the full 3,200 W solar input.

findings.label: AC capacity, idle draw and overload point (Zelpio)
findings.value: AC capacity 83% of rated; idle about 112 W with the inverter on (1,350 Wh in 12 hours, a full battery in about 34 hours); shut off at about 7,200 W
findings.note: Published 2026-08-23. The page names no author and no test load, so this is weaker than the HOBOTECH and Solar Lab figures; quote it as 'Zelpio's review reports'. 2,700 Wh a day is 70% of 3,840 Wh (my arithmetic).

findings.product: Anker SOLIX F3800 (original, same 3,840 Wh / 6,000 W class)
findings.label: Timed run at 5,100 W and surge (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 37 minutes at a 5,100 W load, about 84%; held 7,200 W for roughly 10 s and 8,000 W for 2 to 3 s; 120 V wall charge 2 h 35 min
findings.source_title: Putting the Anker F3800 Power Station to the Test: What Can It ACTUALLY Handle? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: No publication date on the page. This is the predecessor, not the Plus; use it only as context. 5,100 W x 37/60 h = about 3,145 Wh (my arithmetic). Closest thing found to a measured runtime at the question's own 5,000 W.

findings.label: Efficiency, idle draw and charge times (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 84% efficiency; idle about 52 W with the inverter on (about four days to empty); 120 V wall charge a little over 3.5 hours; 3,600 W through the 30 A port, about 1 h 40 min
findings.source_title: Pecron F5000LFP Review: The Best Cheap Power Station for Home Backup? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: No publication date on the page, and no test load given for the 84%. My arithmetic: 0.84 x 5,120 Wh = about 4,300 Wh, about 52 min at 5,000 W. No dB figure; the review calls the fans 'pretty loud'. The page lists the output as 3,600 W at 120 V and 7,200 W at 240 V, and gives no timed full-output test.

findings.value: 0 independent measurements across the four result pages read
findings.source_title: Best home battery backup power station | HoldBackup

Also read the same day: solarwaypoint.com comparison (specs and site estimates only), powerbencher.com best 5000W ('We did not test any of them'; it covers the original F3800 and three sub-5,000 W units), thewattguide.com 5000-watt article ('we have not tested any of these units').

unsourced: Any independent measurement (capacity, efficiency, idle draw, output, noise) of the Nature's Generator L6000: one search returned only the maker's blog and reviews of other products.

Any independent measurement of the EcoFlow TITAN 5000 Plus or TITAN 5000: one search found none, and a search snippet (backuppowerhub.com, not opened) said no independent review existed as of 2026-11-01.

The Solar Lab's idle draw for the Anker F3800 Plus: search snippets gave 47 W and 'around 40 W', but the two Solar Lab F3800 Plus pages I opened carry no idle figure, so it is left out; only Zelpio's 112 W is sourced.
A HOBOTECH capacity test of the Anker F3800 Plus or the Pecron F5000LFP: his Anker tag page lists deal posts only, and a site search returned nothing for Pecron.
Gear Diary's reported 89% efficiency for the OSCAL PowerMax 6000 (review dated 2026-07-31): the page returned 403, so the figure is a search snippet only and is left out.
Popular Mechanics' measurements of the Anker SOLIX S5000 (2026-11-13): the site refused the fetch; the S5000 is a 4,500 W unit and falls outside the line anyway.
Publication dates for The Solar Lab reviews: the pages show only a 2026 copyright line, and my attempts to read the page metadata were blocked.
The test load behind HOBOTECH's capacity figures and the measuring distance for his dB readings: the blog posts do not state them.
Prices and stock for any candidate: not read under this angle.
